title: Light Adapter Proxy LDP API Stencil (scratch)
body:
Purpose:
Quick personal sketch for a very small-surface adapter/proxy that sits between mobile/edge clients and the full Redwood ingress. Goal: minimal wire shape (LDP = lightweight delivery protocol) to enable sandboxed local adapters, feature-gated prewarm, and simpler auth mapping for constrained clients. Not a final spec — thinking-out-loud.

Constraints / design goals:
- Keep request/response shape compact (avoid huge headers)
- Forward compatible: allow arbitrary instrumented fields (telemetry/tracelet) but ignored by default
- Pluggable auth: support bearer, device-assertion, and tenant-proxy tokens
- Low memory/CPU on client adapters; minimal parsing logic
- Deterministic routing hints (tenant, model_family, variant) for quick local routing

High-level flow (text diagram):

Client -> Adapter (LDP) -> Redwood Ingress
  |          |                 |
  | 1: compact LDP request     |
  |--------------------------->|
  |                            | 2: full Redwood API request (expanded)
  |                            |------------------------------->|
  |                            |                                 |
  |                            |<- 3: full Redwood API response  |
  |<- 4: compact LDP response  |

Notes: adapter is allowed to synthesize fields or add a tiny cache key. It MUST NOT mutate client-provided instruction body.

Minimal wire JSON (LDP) - initial proposal (all keys optional but recommended):
{
  "v": "1",                             // protocol version
  "t": "text|chat|embed",             // type hint
  "m": "gptx-small-8k",              // model_family or variant hint
  "tid": "tenant-123",               // tenant or customer id
  "cid": "client-xyz",               // client id (opaque)
  "auth": "b64(token-or-assertion)",// short token or signed assertion
  "p": "<prompt or serialized chat>",// main payload (string or LF-delimited turns)
  "opts": {                             
    "temp": "0.2",
    "max_tokens": "128"
  },
  "meta": "k=v;k2=v2"                // tiny kv string for routing/metrics
}

Why kv-string for meta? to keep parser tiny on C/embedded runtimes. We parse on first pass, host expands into full headers when forwarding.

Adapter responsibilities (sketch):
- Validate v and simple structural sanity (size limits)
- Decode/verify auth (call local KMS or validate signature) – if short bearer, pass through
- Attach routing hints (from meta + config) for fast path selection
- Optional local prewarm: if model hint matches warm set, send a prewarm token to local runtime
- Observe compact telemetry counters (latency, bytes) and sample traces if enabled

Backend expansion (what adapter forwards to Redwood ingress):
- Convert LDP -> Redwood API JSON (standard shapes used in hosted API)
- Add X-Adapter-Meta headers: origin-client, adapter-version, local-latency-ms
- Map adapter auth -> bearer or mTLS credential exchange if tenant requires

Simple example: LDP -> Redwood (pseudocode)
LDP: {v:1,t:text,m:rwkv-mini,p:"Summarize X"} -> Redwood POST /v1/generate {model: "rwkv-mini-v1", input: "Summarize X"} with headers {Authorization: "Bearer <token>"} and trace: adapter:abc, client:client-xyz

Config sketch (adapter local config, TOML-ish):
[adapter]
max_payload_bytes = 65_536
warm_models = ["gptx-small-8k","rwkv-mini"]
allow_forward_all = true
auth_mode = "proxy-token|device-assertion|passthrough"
cache_prefix_ttl_seconds = 30

Routing policy rules (very small DSL idea):
- if meta contains "prod=true" and tenant in allowlist -> route to dedicated cluster
- else if model family matches warm_models -> attempt local runtime first (timeout 40ms) then fallback
- else route to hosted-api with normal SLOs

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Should LDP encode full chat structure as JSON array or keep LF-delimited string? Arrays are nicer but heavier on some embedded parsers.
- Tokenization: do we ever want to include a pre-tokenized size hint? may leak model info but helps batching.
- Encryption: do we require end-to-end encryption or allow adapter to re-encrypt when forwarding? Need legal guidance for some regions.
- Backpressure semantics: if local runtime queues, should adapter accept and return 202 or block? Prefer blocking for UX but need client-configurable timeout.

Failure modes and mitigation:
- Corrupt LDP payload -> 400 + telemetry (bad_payload) and optional debug attachment (first 512 bytes)
- Adapter out-of-memory -> spawn-only mode: respond 503 with Retry-After and forward metric to ops
- Token mapping mismatch -> 401 + detail about expected auth_mode, record sample for forensics

TODO (next steps):
- [ ] Align with security on device-assertion format (Avery)
- [ ] Prototype tiny C parser for LDP string-kv meta (Marco)
- [ ] Run cost estimate for local prewarm budget (Samira)
- [ ] Draft a tiny RFC for the forwarding header contract (concrete header names)

Quick implementation notes / heuristics for prototype:
- Keep core parser < 5k lines of code, no heavy JSON libs on device where possible
- Use base64-url for short tokens to avoid whitespace issues
- Treat opts values as strings to avoid type juggling in small runtimes; coerce on expansion step
- Use a single metrics channel with tagged counters: adapter.bytes_in, adapter.bytes_out, adapter.lat_p50

Snippets to drop into a follow-up RFC:
- Exact LDP schema (v1) with field sizes and mandatory/optional semantics
- Header mapping table LDP field -> Redwood HTTP header or JSON body field
- Security appendix: token lifecycle, rotation, revocation path for adapter-issued tokens

Random thoughts (brain dump):
- Could pair LDP with a tiny binary envelope (TLV) later if string overhead becomes an issue
- Consider a "graceful degrade" boolean where adapter can remove non-essential fields to reduce payload across low-bandwidth links
- Would like an adapter health API: /_healthz returns {uptime, heap, warmed_models} for quick ops checks

If anyone picks this up: please keep changes minimal in first pass. Main value is a tiny, well-documented surface that lets us experiment with on-device adapters without creating large divergence in the Redwood API surface.

End of scratch notes.
